screens.title: Your First C++ Class in Unreal Engine 5
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will create your first C++ Actor class in Unreal Engine 5 and learn how to make code visible and usable inside the Editor and Blueprints. We'll cover why you choose C++ for core logic and when Blueprints make faster iteration, how the Editor's New C++ Class wizard generates header and source files, and the three reflection macros that bridge C++ and the engine: UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION. You will see a concrete walkthrough of a simple AActor called MyFirstActor, learn how to add an editable float and a Blueprint-callable function, and run the actor in a level. I will also point out common mistakes like forgetting the generated header include or omitting UPROPERTY, which prevent editor visibility and garbage collection. By the end you'll understand the actor lifecycle methods BeginPlay and Tick, how to print debug messages from C++, and how to test properties and functions in the Editor. Keep in mind the practical trade-off: use C++ for performance and control, and expose to Blueprints for designer-friendly iteration. What is one small behaviour you might move to Blueprint when you need faster tuning?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and testing
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practice workflows and debugging. You will add UPROPERTY specifiers like EditAnywhere with BlueprintReadWrite so designers can tweak values at runtime and in the Editor. You will implement a BlueprintCallable UFUNCTION to let designers invoke behavior without touching C++. During testing, you will compile from the Editor, drag the actor into the level, and validate that the property appears in the Details Panel and that the function can be invoked. The hands-on activity includes creating MyInteractiveActor with an InteractionRange float and an Interact function that prints which player interacted. Watch for syntax errors in macros and ensure the generated header include is the last include in your header file; missing it is a common compile-time failure. Finally, practicing these steps teaches you a reliable cycle: change C++ → compile → place actor → verify property → call function → read output log. This cycle is the fastest way to iterate while maintaining engine-level performance where it matters.

screens.title: C++ vs Blueprint: when to choose which
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the practical difference between C++ and Blueprints helps you pick the right tool for each task. C++ gives you fine-grained control over memory, performance, and engine-level systems. That makes it the right choice for heavy computations, custom systems, and code you expect to optimize or reuse across many projects. Blueprints excel at rapid iteration and are designed for designers and artists to prototype gameplay quickly without recompiling. The hybrid approach—placing core algorithms in C++ and exposing configuration and event hooks to Blueprints—often delivers the best of both worlds. For example, put complex pathfinding or physics tuning in C++, but expose target parameters and events to Blueprints so designers can tweak behavior in the Editor. A common misconception is that Blueprints are inherently slower for every case; while Blueprints add overhead for some patterns, they are perfectly fine for many gameplay tasks and save development time. In practice, decide by frequency of change and performance requirements: if designers need to tweak values often, expose those values via UPROPERTY and let Blueprints or the Details Panel drive tuning. Reflect on what part of your system must be fast and what part must be adjustable by non-coders.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use C++ for performance and core logic; use Blueprints for fast iteration and designer-facing adjustments; expose C++ to Blueprints where useful.

content.html:
Comparison
C++ vs Blueprint
Trade-offs and a practical hybrid approach
C++ — Strengths
  • Performance-critical systems and complex algorithms.
  • Engine-level changes and precise memory control.
  • Reusable libraries that need strict typing and compile-time checks.
Example
Implementing a custom pathfinding component in C++ for scale and profiling, then exposing tuning parameters to Blueprints.
Blueprints — Strengths
  • Rapid prototyping and visual scripting for designers.
  • Easy to modify in the Editor without compiling.
  • Good for event-driven gameplay and level-specific logic.
Example
Hooking up designer-facing events that respond to in-level triggers and tuning values exposed by C++ properties.
Key takeaway
Prefer a hybrid: keep heavy logic in C++ and expose configuration points with UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION for Blueprint-driven iteration.

screens.title: Create a new C++ class with the Editor wizard
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a new C++ class from the Unreal Editor is a guided process that leaves you with a header and source file ready to edit. Start in the Editor and choose File → New C++ Class. The wizard prompts you to pick a base class; for placeable objects choose Actor. The wizard then asks for a class name—pick something descriptive like MyFirstActor or MyInteractiveActor—and click Create Class. Unreal generates two files with boilerplate: a header with UCLASS and GENERATED_BODY, and a. cpp file with constructor, BeginPlay, and Tick stubs. After generation the files open in your IDE automatically. A useful habit is to inspect the generated header to confirm the '#include "YourClass. generated. h"' is present and last. Another solid practice is to set default values in the constructor rather than in BeginPlay when the default is a stable initial state. For example set a default float value for MyFloatValue inside the constructor. When you save and return to the Editor, compile the project. If compilation succeeds you can drag the new actor from the Content Browser into the level and test its defaults and behavior. This step-by-step ensures the Editor and reflection system recognize your class.

keyIdea.title: Create flow
keyIdea.text: Use the New C++ Class wizard, choose Actor, name your class, inspect generated files, set defaults in the constructor, then compile and place the actor.

content.html:
Process Flow
Create a new C++ class
Wizard steps and best practices
Steps
1. File → New C++ Class
Open the wizard and pick a base class, typically Actor for placeable objects.
2. Choose name and module
Give a clear name like MyFirstActor. Confirm the project module and click Create.
3. Inspect generated files
Verify UCLASS and GENERATED_BODY are present and generated header include is last.
4. Set defaults and compile
Set default values in the constructor and compile from the Editor.
Best practice
Set stable defaults in the constructor, and reserve BeginPlay for runtime initialization that depends on other objects or the level.
Quick example
Set 'MyFloatValue = 100.0f' in the constructor so the default appears in the Details Panel when you place the actor.
Misconception
Don't place runtime-dependent initialization in the constructor; components or actors might not be ready until BeginPlay.

screens.title: What is AActor and common base classes
screens.narratorSegment: AActor is the base class for anything you can place or spawn in a level. That includes props, lights, and interactive objects. APawn is a subclass used for player-controlled or AI-controlled entities and provides the interface for possession and movement. ACharacter further specializes Pawn with built-in character movement components and standard movement replication. UActorComponent is not an Actor but a reusable object that attaches to an Actor to provide functionality like health, inventory, or custom behavior. When designing your first class, choose Actor when you need a placeable object without character movement. If you are implementing player-driven movement or AI, consider APawn or ACharacter. Use UActorComponent when you want to share logic across multiple actors without inheritance. For example, implement a reusable InteractionComponent that multiple actors can attach to instead of copying code between Actor subclasses. A common misunderstanding is to overuse inheritance for shared features; composition with components is often more flexible and cleaner for reuse. Choose the smallest, most focused base class that provides the features you need and add components for shared behavior. What is AActor and common base classes means pick aactor for placeable objects, apawn/acharacter for controllable entities, and uactorcomponent for reusable, attachable behavior.. In practical terms, aactor, apawn, acharacter, and uactorcomponent explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Pick AActor for placeable objects, APawn/ACharacter for controllable entities, and UActorComponent for reusable, attachable behavior.

content.html:
Definition
AActor and related classes
Understand purpose and when to use each base type
AActor
Base for any placeable or spawnable object. Use for props, lights, interactive objects without specialized movement.
APawn
Used for entities that can be possessed and controlled by players or AI. Provides possession hooks and basic movement interfaces.
ACharacter
A Pawn specialized for humanoid movement. Includes CharacterMovementComponent for walking, jumping, and replication behavior.
UActorComponent
Attach to Actors to share functionality across different actor types. Prefer composition with components rather than deep inheritance for reuse.
Design tip
If multiple actors need the same feature, implement it as a component and attach where needed instead of duplicating code across actor subclasses.

screens.title: UCLASS: purpose and common specifiers
screens.narratorSegment: UCLASS marks a C++ class so Unreal's reflection system can recognize, serialize, and manage it. Without UCLASS your class won't appear in the Editor, won't participate in garbage collection, and cannot expose properties or methods to Blueprints. Inside the UCLASS parentheses you can add specifiers that change how the class interacts with the Editor and Blueprints. Two common specifiers are Blueprintable, which allows Blueprint classes to inherit from this C++ class, and BlueprintType, which allows variables of this class to be used in Blueprints. For most gameplay classes you will include both to enable flexible use by designers. A typical declaration looks like UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType). Remember that GENERATED_BODY() must appear inside the class declaration; it expands to necessary boilerplate for reflection. A common misconception is that UCLASS alone is enough for all exposure; it is not. You still need UPROPERTY for variables and UFUNCTION for functions to expose members. Think of UCLASS as the gate that makes the class visible to the engine, and the other macros as switches that expose individual members. UCLASS: purpose and common specifiers means uclass registers the class with unreal's reflection system; specifiers like blueprintable and blueprinttype control blueprint inheritance and usage.. In practical terms, how uclass enables reflection and what blueprintable / blueprinttype do. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UCLASS role

content.html:
Definition
UCLASS()
Make your class known to the engine
What it does
  • Registers the class with reflection and garbage collection systems.
  • Allows the Editor to instantiate and serialize instances.
  • Is required before using UPROPERTY or UFUNCTION on members.
Common specifiers
Blueprintable — lets Blueprints inherit from the class.
BlueprintType — allows variables of this type in Blueprints.
Misconception
UCLASS alone does not expose properties or methods. You must still mark variables with UPROPERTY and methods with UFUNCTION to make them visible to the Editor and Blueprints.

screens.title: UPROPERTY: expose variables to Editor and Blueprints
screens.narratorSegment: UPROPERTY is the macro that makes C++ member variables visible to the Editor and to Blueprints, and it also informs the engine's garbage collector about object references. Choosing the correct specifiers determines how designers can use the variable. EditAnywhere lets a variable be edited in the Details Panel for any instance of the actor; VisibleAnywhere makes it visible but not editable. BlueprintReadOnly allows Blueprints to read the value but not modify it; BlueprintReadWrite allows both read and write. Another useful specifier is Category which groups the property in the Details Panel under a custom header, for example Category="Interaction". Always consider who will use the variable: if designers need to tweak it, use EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite. If the value should be shown but not adjusted, choose VisibleAnywhere and BlueprintReadOnly. A common mistake is forgetting UPROPERTY entirely; the variable will not appear in the Editor, and pointers to UObject-derived types may be invisible to the garbage collector, causing lifecycle issues. Use UPROPERTY both to enable editing and to ensure safe object references. UPROPERTY: expose variables to Editor and Blueprints means uproperty exposes variables to the editor and blueprints and protects uobject references for garbage collection; choose specifiers based on editability and blueprint access.. In practical terms, specifiers like editanywhere, visibleanywhere, blueprintreadonly, and blueprintreadwrite. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
UPROPERTY()
Expose and protect member variables
Common specifiers
  • EditAnywhere — editable in Details for any instance.
  • VisibleAnywhere — visible but not editable.
  • BlueprintReadOnly / BlueprintReadWrite — control Blueprint access.
UI organization
Use Category="My Properties" to group related fields in the Details Panel so designers can find them quickly.
Example
// MyFirstActor.h (excerpt)
UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "My Properties")
float MyFloatValue;

screens.title: UFUNCTION: expose methods and network specifiers
screens.narratorSegment: UFUNCTION lets you expose C++ methods to Blueprints and the engine. Use BlueprintCallable for functions you want designers to call from Blueprint graphs or from the Details Panel when the Editor supports it. Use BlueprintPure for getter-style functions that do not modify state and simply return a value; pure functions have no execution pins in Blueprint. In addition, Unreal provides networking specifiers such as Server, Client, and NetMulticast to control where a function runs across the network, but those are relevant when implementing multiplayer. For this chapter, the key is to mark interactive functions you want designers to invoke with BlueprintCallable and to categorize them with Category = "My Functions" for organization. A concrete example is PrintMyMessage, which we mark BlueprintCallable so it can be invoked from Blueprints or seen as an Editor-callable action. A common misconception is to expect UFUNCTION alone to expose property-like behavior; functions must still follow the engine rules for parameters and return types that Blueprints can handle. Keep signatures simple when you intend them for Blueprint usage. UFUNCTION: expose methods and network specifiers means mark methods with ufunction to expose them to blueprints; use blueprintcallable for actions and blueprintpure for read-only getters.. In practical terms, blueprintcallable, blueprintpure and a note on networking specifiers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Header walkthrough: MyFirstActor.h
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the header for MyFirstActor to see how to declare properties and functions for Editor exposure. The header begins with standard includes and the generated header include which must come last. The UCLASS macro, often with Blueprintable and BlueprintType, tells the engine to register the class. Inside the class, GENERATED_BODY expands required reflection boilerplate. Public members include the constructor declaration and UPROPERTY declarations. In our example we add a float MyFloatValue with EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite so designers can edit and Blueprints can modify it. We also declare a UFUNCTION called PrintMyMessage marked BlueprintCallable so it can be invoked from Blueprints or the Editor. Protected and public virtual functions include BeginPlay and Tick, which the engine calls at lifecycle points. A common mistake is to forget GENERATED_BODY or to place the generated include in the wrong order; both cause build errors or missing reflection data. When you declare properties and functions clearly in the header, the Editor's Details Panel and Blueprint menus will reflect those choices after a successful compile. UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType)

};

Code Walkthrough
MyFirstActor.cpp
Constructor, BeginPlay, Tick, and a callable method
// MyFirstActor.cpp
#include "MyFirstActor.h"
#include "Engine/Engine.h" // For GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage

AMyFirstActor::AMyFirstActor()
{
	PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
	MyFloatValue = 100.0f; // default value
}

void AMyFirstActor::BeginPlay()
{
	Super::BeginPlay();
	if (GEngine)
	{
		GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Green, TEXT("MyFirstActor has begun play!"));
	}
	UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("MyFirstActor has begun play from C++ log!"));
}

void AMyFirstActor::Tick(float DeltaTime)
{
	Super::Tick(DeltaTime);
	// per-frame logic
}

void AMyFirstActor::PrintMyMessage()
{
	if (GEngine)
	{
		GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Yellow, FString::Printf(TEXT("MyFloatValue is: %f"), MyFloatValue));
	}
	UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("PrintMyMessage called. MyFloatValue: %f"), MyFloatValue);
}
Runtime checks
  • Verify GEngine is valid before calling AddOnScreenDebugMessage.
  • Only enable Tick when required to avoid unnecessary frame work.
  • Use UE_LOG for persistent logging in the Output Log.

Call PrintMyMessage from the Editor or Blueprint to show MyFloatValue on the screen and in the log for quick verification.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: When working with Unreal C++, certain mistakes recur and are easy to fix once you know them. First, forgetting '#include "YourClass. generated. h"' or placing it before other includes often leads to cryptic compiler errors or missing reflection data. Always include the generated header as the last include line in your header. Second, forgetting UPROPERTY or UFUNCTION prevents the Editor and Blueprints from seeing your members; a variable without UPROPERTY will not show up in the Details Panel and UObject pointers may not be tracked by the garbage collector. Third, enabling Tick without needing per-frame updates costs performance—set PrimaryActorTick. bCanEverTick to true only when necessary. Finally, watch your UFUNCTION signatures: keep parameter and return types Blueprint-friendly when you plan to call them from Blueprint. For debugging, use UE_LOG and AddOnScreenDebugMessage to surface values during BeginPlay and function calls. If a property or function doesn't appear after compiling, re-open the Editor's Content Browser to refresh asset metadata, check the build logs, and verify your macros and include order. These checks resolve most integration issues quickly. In practical terms, missing macros, include order, and unnecessary tick usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should carry forward. First, AActor is the base for placeable objects; choose APawn or ACharacter when you need possession and movement. Second, UCLASS marks a type for the engine's reflection system; it is the gatekeeper that enables editor visibility and serialization. Third, UPROPERTY exposes variables to the Details Panel and Blueprints and informs garbage collection—choose specifiers like EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite when designers must edit values. Fourth, UFUNCTION makes methods callable from Blueprints; use BlueprintCallable for actions and BlueprintPure for read-only getters. Finally, remember the lifecycle: set stable defaults in the constructor, use BeginPlay for runtime initialization, and only enable Tick when per-frame updates are required. These rules form a repeatable workflow: declare macros in headers, implement behavior in source, compile, place the actor, and validate using on-screen messages and the Output Log. Keep iterating with small changes and use components for shared functionality to avoid brittle inheritance hierarchies.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will create your first C++ Actor class in Unreal Engine 5 and learn how to make code visible and usable inside the Editor and Blueprints. We'll cover why you choose C++ for core logic and when Blueprints make faster iteration, how the Editor's New C++ Class wizard generates header and source files, and the three reflection macros that bridge C++ and the engine: UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION. You will see a concrete walkthrough of a simple AActor called MyFirstActor, learn how to add an editable float and a Blueprint-callable function, and run the actor in a level. I will also point out common mistakes like forgetting the generated header include or omitting UPROPERTY, which prevent editor visibility and garbage collection. By the end you'll understand the actor lifecycle methods BeginPlay and Tick, how to print debug messages from C++, and how to test properties and functions in the Editor. Keep in mind the practical trade-off: use C++ for performance and control, and expose to Blueprints for designer-friendly iteration. What is one small behaviour you might move to Blueprint when you need faster tuning?

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to distinguish when to use C++ versus Blueprints, create a new C++ Actor class from the Unreal Editor wizard, and expose members to the Editor and Blueprints using Unreal's reflection macros. You will add UPROPERTY variables and UFUNCTION methods, compile, place the actor in a level, and observe lifecycle events like BeginPlay and Tick. This chapter also prepares you to choose sensible specifiers—for example, EditAnywhere with BlueprintReadWrite for values designers can edit and change—and shows how to test functions from the Details Panel. These skills matter because exposing the right parts of your C++ code makes iteration faster for artists and safer for systems-level code. A practical example you will try is creating MyInteractiveActor with an editable InteractionRange and a BlueprintCallable Interact function. Finally, you will learn common mistakes to avoid, such as omitting the generated header include or forgetting macros, which prevent the Editor from recognizing your class and properties.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice workflows and debugging. You will add UPROPERTY specifiers like EditAnywhere with BlueprintReadWrite so designers can tweak values at runtime and in the Editor. You will implement a BlueprintCallable UFUNCTION to let designers invoke behavior without touching C++. During testing, you will compile from the Editor, drag the actor into the level, and validate that the property appears in the Details Panel and that the function can be invoked. The hands-on activity includes creating MyInteractiveActor with an InteractionRange float and an Interact function that prints which player interacted. Watch for syntax errors in macros and ensure the generated header include is the last include in your header file; missing it is a common compile-time failure. Finally, practicing these steps teaches you a reliable cycle: change C++ → compile → place actor → verify property → call function → read output log. This cycle is the fastest way to iterate while maintaining engine-level performance where it matters.

Understanding the practical difference between C++ and Blueprints helps you pick the right tool for each task. C++ gives you fine-grained control over memory, performance, and engine-level systems. That makes it the right choice for heavy computations, custom systems, and code you expect to optimize or reuse across many projects. Blueprints excel at rapid iteration and are designed for designers and artists to prototype gameplay quickly without recompiling. The hybrid approach—placing core algorithms in C++ and exposing configuration and event hooks to Blueprints—often delivers the best of both worlds. For example, put complex pathfinding or physics tuning in C++, but expose target parameters and events to Blueprints so designers can tweak behavior in the Editor. A common misconception is that Blueprints are inherently slower for every case; while Blueprints add overhead for some patterns, they are perfectly fine for many gameplay tasks and save development time. In practice, decide by frequency of change and performance requirements: if designers need to tweak values often, expose those values via UPROPERTY and let Blueprints or the Details Panel drive tuning. AActor is the base class for anything you can place or spawn in a level. That includes props, lights, and interactive objects. APawn is a subclass used for player-controlled or AI-controlled entities and provides the interface for possession and movement. ACharacter further specializes Pawn with built-in character movement components and standard movement replication. UActorComponent is not an Actor but a reusable object that attaches to an Actor to provide functionality like health, inventory, or custom behavior. When designing your first class, choose Actor when you need a placeable object without character movement. If you are implementing player-driven movement or AI, consider APawn or ACharacter. Use UActorComponent when you want to share logic across multiple actors without inheritance. For example, implement a reusable InteractionComponent that multiple actors can attach to instead of copying code between Actor subclasses. A common misunderstanding is to overuse inheritance for shared features; composition with components is often more flexible and cleaner for reuse. Choose the smallest, most focused base class that provides the features you need and add components for shared behavior. UCLASS marks a C++ class so Unreal's reflection system can recognize, serialize, and manage it. Without UCLASS your class won't appear in the Editor, won't participate in garbage collection, and cannot expose properties or methods to Blueprints. Inside the UCLASS parentheses you can add specifiers that change how the class interacts with the Editor and Blueprints. Two common specifiers are Blueprintable, which allows Blueprint classes to inherit from this C++ class, and BlueprintType, which allows variables of this class to be used in Blueprints. For most gameplay classes you will include both to enable flexible use by designers. A typical declaration looks like UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType). Remember that GENERATED_BODY() must appear inside the class declaration; it expands to necessary boilerplate for reflection. A common misconception is that UCLASS alone is enough for all exposure; it is not. You still need UPROPERTY for variables and UFUNCTION for functions to expose members. Think of UCLASS as the gate that makes the class visible to the engine, and the other macros as switches that expose individual members. UPROPERTY is the macro that makes C++ member variables visible to the Editor and to Blueprints, and it also informs the engine's garbage collector about object references. Choosing the correct specifiers determines how designers can use the variable. EditAnywhere lets a variable be edited in the Details Panel for any instance of the actor; VisibleAnywhere makes it visible but not editable. BlueprintReadOnly allows Blueprints to read the value but not modify it; BlueprintReadWrite allows both read and write. Another useful specifier is Category which groups the property in the Details Panel under a custom header, for example Category="Interaction". Always consider who will use the variable: if designers need to tweak it, use EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite. If the value should be shown but not adjusted, choose VisibleAnywhere and BlueprintReadOnly. A common mistake is forgetting UPROPERTY entirely; the variable will not appear in the Editor, and pointers to UObject-derived types may be invisible to the garbage collector, causing lifecycle issues. Use UPROPERTY both to enable editing and to ensure safe object references. UFUNCTION lets you expose C++ methods to Blueprints and the engine. Use BlueprintCallable for functions you want designers to call from Blueprint graphs or from the Details Panel when the Editor supports it. Use BlueprintPure for getter-style functions that do not modify state and simply return a value; pure functions have no execution pins in Blueprint. In addition, Unreal provides networking specifiers such as Server, Client, and NetMulticast to control where a function runs across the network, but those are relevant when implementing multiplayer. For this chapter, the key is to mark interactive functions you want designers to invoke with BlueprintCallable and to categorize them with Category = "My Functions" for organization. A concrete example is PrintMyMessage, which we mark BlueprintCallable so it can be invoked from Blueprints or seen as an Editor-callable action. A common misconception is to expect UFUNCTION alone to expose property-like behavior; functions must still follow the engine rules for parameters and return types that Blueprints can handle. Keep signatures simple when you intend them for Blueprint usage. When working with Unreal C++, certain mistakes recur and are easy to fix once you know them. First, forgetting '#include "YourClass. generated. h"' or placing it before other includes often leads to cryptic compiler errors or missing reflection data. Always include the generated header as the last include line in your header. Second, forgetting UPROPERTY or UFUNCTION prevents the Editor and Blueprints from seeing your members; a variable without UPROPERTY will not show up in the Details Panel and UObject pointers may not be tracked by the garbage collector. Third, enabling Tick without needing per-frame updates costs performance—set PrimaryActorTick. bCanEverTick to true only when necessary. Finally, watch your UFUNCTION signatures: keep parameter and return types Blueprint-friendly when you plan to call them from Blueprint. For debugging, use UE_LOG and AddOnScreenDebugMessage to surface values during BeginPlay and function calls. If a property or function doesn't appear after compiling, re-open the Editor's Content Browser to refresh asset metadata, check the build logs, and verify your macros and include order. These checks resolve most integration issues quickly. Let's summarize the essential concepts you should carry forward. First, AActor is the base for placeable objects; choose APawn or ACharacter when you need possession and movement. Second, UCLASS marks a type for the engine's reflection system; it is the gatekeeper that enables editor visibility and serialization. Third, UPROPERTY exposes variables to the Details Panel and Blueprints and informs garbage collection—choose specifiers like EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite when designers must edit values. Fourth, UFUNCTION makes methods callable from Blueprints; use BlueprintCallable for actions and BlueprintPure for read-only getters. Finally, remember the lifecycle: set stable defaults in the constructor, use BeginPlay for runtime initialization, and only enable Tick when per-frame updates are required. These rules form a repeatable workflow: declare macros in headers, implement behavior in source, compile, place the actor, and validate using on-screen messages and the Output Log. Keep iterating with small changes and use components for shared functionality to avoid brittle inheritance hierarchies.

A final quick reference to keep nearby while you code. First, always include the generated header as the last include in your header files; missing or misordered generated includes cause reflection and compile problems. Second, choose UPROPERTY specifiers based on who needs to change a value: EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite for designer-editable fields, VisibleAnywhere and BlueprintReadOnly when you want visibility but no editing. Third, only enable Tick if you require per-frame logic; unnecessary Tick usage increases C P U load. These concise rules reduce common integration errors and make your workflow predictable: declare with macros, implement behavior, compile, verify in the Editor, and iterate. When in doubt, prefer composition with components for shared behavior, and expose only the configuration points designers need.
